title: Energy Management & the Set as a Story
skill: Plan a set's energy as a narrative arc that builds, peaks and releases on purpose.
content:
Energy is the real medium

You are not just mixing records, you are sculpting a curve of physical and emotional intensity over time. Every track sits somewhere on an energy scale, and your job is to move the room up and down that scale on purpose, not by accident. Think of a set as a story with an opening, rising action, a climax and a release. A flat line bores people; a wall of peak-time bangers exhausts them in twenty minutes and leaves you nowhere to go.

Score your tracks 1-10

Before a gig, give every track an energy rating. Energy is not the same as BPM. A stripped 124 BPM tech-house roller can read as a 4, while a euphoric 124 BPM vocal track with a huge riser reads as an 8. Rate on perceived intensity: density of the arrangement, presence of vocals/melody, drop weight, and how hard the kick hits. Tag these in your software (colour or a custom 'Energy' column) so you can see them at a glance.

EnergyFeelTypical use
1-3Atmospheric, sparse, dubbyOpening, palette cleanser after a peak
4-6Grooving, head-nodding, rollingBuilding the floor, connective tissue
7-8Driving, hands-up, vocal hooksPre-peak and sustained dancing
9-10Anthem, full drop, maximumThe climax — used sparingly

The arc, not the staircase

Beginners climb a straight staircase: each track louder and harder than the last until they hit 10 with forty minutes still to play. Pros build in waves. You climb three or four tracks, then deliberately pull back one or two points to give the crowd a breath, then climb higher than before. Each dip makes the next peak feel bigger by contrast. The overall trend rises, but it is jagged, not linear. Tension and release is the entire game — a drop only hits because something quieter came before it.

Save your bombs. If you play your three biggest records in the first half hour, the back half of your set has no ceiling left. Hold at least one or two genuine 10s in reserve for the moment the room is fullest and most ready.

Tools for moving energy

  • Within a track: filter sweeps, loop the breakdown to extend tension, cut the bass to create lift before a drop.
  • Across tracks: raise or lower the energy rating of the next selection; nudge BPM up a couple of points over several tracks to quietly accelerate the room.
  • Arrangement: a long breakdown is a built-in energy dip — use the producer's work instead of fighting it.

Map the whole set

For a recorded mix or a known slot, sketch the curve on paper first: where is the opening plateau, where is the first wave, where is the climax, where is the comedown. You will deviate live based on the room, but having a planned shape stops you from peaking too early or wandering aimlessly. The single most common amateur mistake is no shape at all — just a pile of good tracks played back to back with no relationship between them.
exercise: Build a 60-minute energy map. Pick 12 tracks, rate each 1-10 for energy, then arrange them into a curve that climbs in two or three waves to a single climax around minute 45 before easing off. Record the mix and plot the actual energy you hear against your plan to see where you peaked too soon.

tracks.why: A long slow-burn builder — study how it climbs from a 3 to an 8 across one track, modelling the arc you want across a set.

tracks.why: A masterclass in patient tension and release — the extended build teaches you how restraint makes the eventual peak land.

title: Reading the Room in Real Time
skill: Read dancefloor feedback live and adjust your next track choice to keep people moving.
content:
The floor is talking — learn to listen

A planned set is a hypothesis. The room is the experiment. Reading the room means continuously gathering feedback from the dancefloor and adjusting your next one or two tracks to match what is actually happening, not what you hoped would happen. The DJs who clear floors are usually the ones playing their plan no matter what they see.

The signals, ranked by reliability

SignalMeansReliability
Feet moving / dancingYou are connectingHigh
Crowd density at the frontPeople pulled toward youHigh
Hands up on the dropPeak engagementHigh
Heads turning to the boothCuriosity, 'what is this?'Medium
Phones out filmingA moment is landingMedium
Drifting to the bar / exitsYou are losing themHigh (negative)
Talking, checking phonesDisengagedMedium (negative)

Watch feet, not faces

Faces lie and lighting hides them. Feet do not. Scan the floor in a slow sweep every thirty seconds or so: are people moving, and is the moving area growing or shrinking? A small but locked-in, dancing crowd is a far better signal than a large crowd standing still. Pay special attention to the moment a new track's drop hits — that first reaction tells you whether your read was right.

Give a track time before you judge it. Do not panic-mix out the second a track does not instantly explode. Many records need 60-90 seconds to land. Bailing early trains you to only play obvious bangers and kills any sense of journey.

The feedback loop

  1. Observe the floor's response to the track that is playing now.
  2. Interpret — is energy rising, holding or sagging?
  3. Decide the next track: hold the vibe, push higher, or pull back and regroup.
  4. Always have two cued options — a 'keep climbing' track and a 'safe, known' track — so you are never caught flat-footed.

When you are losing them

If the floor sags, resist the urge to immediately drop your biggest record to rescue it — that burns your ammunition and often reads as desperate. First try a track with a stronger, more familiar groove or a recognisable vocal hook to re-engage. Reset the energy to a solid 5-6 that people can lock into, then rebuild. Sometimes the fix is simply a four-on-the-floor track with a clear, danceable rhythm after you wandered too far into something cerebral.

Read the context, not just the moment

Factor in time of night, how drunk the room is, the temperature, and whether it is a Tuesday or a Saturday. The same track that empties a 11pm warm-up floor will detonate a 1am peak. Reading the room is reading the whole situation, then trusting your eyes over your ego.
exercise: Run a live read-and-adjust drill. At your next gig or practice with friends, commit to changing your planned next track at least three times based purely on what the floor does. After each change, note in one line what signal prompted it and whether the new choice worked.

tracks.why: A near-universal floor-filler — useful as your 'safe re-engage' card to study how a familiar hook instantly pulls a drifting crowd back.

title: Programming by Key, BPM, Genre & Vibe
skill: Group tracks by key, BPM, genre and vibe so compatible records are always at your fingertips.
content:
Programming is pre-mixing

Half of a great set is decided before you touch a fader, in how your library is organised. Programming means arranging your collection so that, at any moment, you can instantly find a track that is compatible with what is playing on four axes: key, BPM, genre and vibe. Get this right and live mixing becomes choosing between good options rather than frantically scrolling.

The four compatibility axes

AxisCompatible rangeWhy it matters
BPMWithin ~3-4 BPM, or half/double timeBeatmatchable without obvious pitch artefacts
KeySame, +/-1 on the Camelot wheel, or relative major/minorAvoids clashing notes when layered
GenreSame or adjacent (tech-house to house)Keeps groove and drum feel consistent
VibeSimilar energy/moodKeeps the narrative coherent

Key and the Camelot wheel

Let your software analyse keys and display them in Camelot notation (8A, 9B etc.). The simple rules: same number same letter is a perfect match; same number different letter (8A to 8B) is the energy-boost relative major/minor jump; one number up or down same letter (8A to 9A or 7A) is a smooth neighbour. Stay inside that circle and you will rarely get a dissonant clash. This matters most when you layer tracks, hold long blends, or use acapellas — for quick cuts on the drop, key matters less.

Organise so the work is already done

  • BPM crates or smart playlists: auto-group ranges like 120-124, 124-128, 128-132 so you are never reaching across a 10 BPM gap by accident.
  • Colour by energy or vibe: e.g. blue = deep/atmospheric, green = groovy, orange = driving, red = peak. One glance tells you a track's role.
  • Genre / sub-genre tags: tag rather than hard-foldering, so a disco-house track can live in both 'disco' and 'house' searches.
  • 'Vibe' tags: free-text like 'sunset', 'dark', 'vocal', 'tool', 'bomb' — these capture what no automatic field can.
Trust the analysis, but verify the key. Automatic key detection is usually 85-90% accurate but stumbles on tracks with ambiguous tonality or key changes. For your most-used records, confirm the key by ear or against a second source before relying on it for a tight harmonic blend.

Build bridges between groups

The real skill is connecting groups so you can travel across your library. Identify 'bridge' tracks: a record that sits between two genres or that works at the top of one BPM band and the bottom of the next. These are how you move from deep house into techno, or from 124 to 130, without a jarring jump. Tag them so you can find the door when you need it.

Smart playlists do the sorting

Set up rules-based smart playlists: 'house AND 124-128 BPM AND energy 6-8' instantly surfaces your pre-peak house weapons. Maintain these once and they update themselves as you add music, turning a chaotic library into a programmed, gig-ready instrument.
exercise: Build a four-track harmonic chain. Pick a starting track, then use the Camelot wheel to find a same-key, a relative major/minor, and a neighbour track, all within 4 BPM. Mix through all four and listen for any clashing notes in the blends to confirm your key choices are right.

title: Pacing: Warm-Up vs Peak vs Closing Slots
skill: Pace a set differently for warm-up, peak-time and closing slots so you serve the room, not your ego.
content:
The slot defines the job

The same DJ should play completely differently depending on where they sit in the night. The single fastest way to never get re-booked is to treat a warm-up slot like a peak slot. Pacing means matching your energy, track selection and tempo to the function of your slot, which means swallowing your ego and serving the night's overall arc.

Three slots, three jobs

SlotJobTypical energyTempo posture
Warm-upSet mood, fill the floor gently, hand over a warm room2-5Lower end, leave headroom above you
PeakMaximum sustained energy, the biggest moments7-10Top of the night's range
ClosingBring it down gracefully, send them home happy6 down to 3Ease back, more vocal/emotional

Warm-up: the discipline of restraint

The warm-up DJ's enemy is impatience. Your job is to build a foundation, not to show off. Play deeper, groovier, lower-energy material and crucially leave tempo and intensity headroom for the headliner. If you are on before a peak DJ who plays at 128, do not warm up at 128 with peak-energy tracks — play 122-125, grooving and atmospheric, so the room has somewhere to go. Avoid the obvious anthems entirely; the moment you drop the night's biggest record at 11pm, you have stolen it from the person whose slot it was. A great warm-up is judged by how easy you made the next DJ's job.

Reading the headliner. Find out who plays after you and roughly what tempo and style they open with. Aim to hand the room over at a tempo and energy a notch below their opening, so their first track is a natural step up, not a collision or a drop.

Peak: deliver, then sustain

Peak-time is what people remember, but the mistake is treating it as one long maximum. Even within peak you need micro-waves — climb to a 10, release to a 7, climb again — or you flatline the room's ability to feel intensity. Play your strongest, most recognisable, hardest-hitting material, keep transitions tight and confident, and use double drops, FX builds and big vocal moments. The energy floor is high but the contour still matters.

Closing: the graceful descent

The closing slot is the most under-rated and the hardest to do well. The peak is over; ramming bangers into an emptying room is desperate and tone-deaf. Your job is the comedown: gradually lower energy and tempo, lean into emotional, vocal, nostalgic and 'last song of the night' records. Give people the bittersweet, memorable ending that makes them want to come back. The final track should feel like a deliberate full stop, not the music simply running out.

Pacing within any slot

Whatever the slot, never spend your whole arc in the first third of it. A 90-minute set that hits its ceiling at minute 25 has nowhere to live for 65 minutes. Pace your climb to the length of your slot — longer slots demand more patience early.
exercise: Record a warm-up set with a hard ceiling. Play 30 minutes targeting energy 2-5 and a tempo of 122-124, with a rule that you may not play any track you would consider a peak anthem. The challenge is keeping it interesting and groovy while deliberately leaving headroom above you.

title: Preparing Crates & Track IDs for a Specific Gig
skill: Build a focused crate and shortlist of track IDs tailored to a specific gig and crowd.
content:
Prep beats talent on the night

Walking into a gig with your entire 5,000-track library and no plan is a recipe for panic-scrolling and safe, boring choices. Gig-specific preparation means building a focused crate — typically two to three times more tracks than you can actually play — curated to the venue, slot, crowd and the other DJs on the bill. A 90-minute set is roughly 18-22 tracks; prepare 40-60 strong options and you have room to react without drowning in choice.

Research the gig first

  • Venue and sound system: a big club rig handles sub-heavy material a small bar PA will turn to mud.
  • Slot and timing: warm-up, peak or close (see lesson 4) dictates energy entirely.
  • Crowd: age, scene, how 'heads' vs 'general public' — local promoters or past flyers tell you a lot.
  • The other DJs: know what is played before and after you so you do not clash or duplicate tracks.

Layer the crate

Structure your gig crate in three layers so you can navigate it instantly under pressure:

  1. Core (must-play): 8-12 tracks you are fairly sure you will play and that anchor the set.
  2. Flex (probable): 20-30 tracks grouped by energy/BPM band to push higher, hold, or pull back as the room dictates.
  3. Safety net (rescue): 6-10 known crowd-pleasers for if you are losing the floor, plus a couple of genuine bombs for the big moment.
Prep the cue points, not just the tracklist. For every track in the gig crate, confirm the beatgrid is correct and set/verify your intro and drop hot cues. Discovering a wrong beatgrid mid-blend in front of a packed room is a self-inflicted disaster. Do this at home, not in the booth.

Track IDs and your shortlist

Keep a running 'ID list' — a notes file of new tracks you want to try, where you found them, and which gig they suit. Before each gig, pull the relevant IDs into the crate and tag them clearly (e.g. colour 'untested') so you know which records carry risk. Play tested weapons in the high-stakes moments and slot the untested IDs into lower-risk windows where a miss costs little.

Physical and file readiness

ItemCheck before you leave
USB drivesTwo identical exported copies, both tested on the club platform
Export formatExported for the right software (Rekordbox/Serato/Engine)
Crate visibleGig crate is at the top of the list, clearly named with the date
Cue pointsAll saved and confirmed transferred to the export

Curate ruthlessly

The discipline is leaving tracks out. A tight, intentional crate of 50 tracks you trust beats a sprawling 400-track dump every time. If a record does not have a clear job in this room on this night, it does not belong in this crate.
exercise: Build a full gig crate for an imaginary booking. Choose a specific venue, slot and crowd, then assemble a named crate of 40-50 tracks split into core, flex and safety-net layers, with energy and BPM tags on each. Verify the beatgrid and intro/drop cues on at least ten of them.

title: Handling Requests & Seizing the Big Moment
skill: Field crowd requests gracefully and recognize the exact moment to drop your biggest track.
content:
Requests: politics, not just music

A request is rarely about the specific song — it is someone wanting to feel heard and to have a moment. How you handle the human matters as much as whether you play the track. The goal is to stay in control of your set while leaving the requester feeling respected, not dismissed.

A decision framework for requests

SituationResponse
Request fits the vibe and you have itPlay it — possibly soon, possibly later when it lands best
Fits but wrong moment'Great track, I'll work it in' — then actually do, or play something adjacent
Does not fit at allWarm decline: 'Not quite right for this room tonight, but I've got something you'll love coming'
Aggressive / repeated demandsStay calm, brief, never argue; signal to security if needed
Never let a requester touch the gear or stand in the booth. Smile, nod, lean in to hear them, then turn back to your set. A friendly two-second acknowledgement defuses 90% of requesters; a dismissive wave or an argument escalates them.

The art of the graceful decline

You are the curator, and playing every request would shred your set's narrative. But 'no' costs you nothing if it is warm. Acknowledge the person, give a tiny reason tied to the room ('it'd kill the energy right now'), and offer a bridge ('but stick around, the next twenty minutes are for you'). People accept being told no by someone who clearly has a plan; they resent being ignored. Reading a request also feeds your room-read — if three people ask for the same kind of track, the floor may be telling you something.

Seizing the big moment

The flip side of restraint is knowing exactly when to unleash. Your biggest record — the anthem, the double-drop, the track everyone knows — only detonates if the moment is ripe. The ingredients of the right moment:

  • The floor is full and locked in — maximum people to share it.
  • Energy is already high (a 7-8) so the bomb pushes it to 10 rather than starting cold.
  • A natural arrival point — end of a build, the top of a wave, a moment of collective anticipation you have manufactured.
  • Time of night aligns — peak-time, not the warm-up.

Manufacture the moment, then deliver

Great DJs do not wait passively for the perfect moment — they build it. Stack tension with a long filtered breakdown, loop a build, cut the music to near-silence for a beat, then drop the anthem on the downbeat so the room erupts. Lock the incoming track's first downbeat, kill any clashing bass, and hit it clean. A fluffed beatgrid or a late drop deflates the exact moment you spent five minutes constructing. When you nail it, you do not need to do it again for a while — one perfectly-timed bomb is worth more than five thrown out at random.
exercise: Practice building and dropping the big moment. Take your single biggest crowd-known track, then construct a two-minute build into it using a filter sweep or extended breakdown loop on the previous track, cutting to a brief drop in energy right before the downbeat. Time the drop so it lands exactly on the one, and record it to check your build actually created tension.
